## Neither — and please don't make tonight the observation period.

**Don't feed him anything, and please get him seen tonight rather than in the morning.** If at any point he develops a swollen/firm/tense belly, fever, blood or black tarry stool, vomiting (especially green/bile-stained or bloody), drooling or trouble swallowing or breathing, refusal of a food he normally loves, lethargy/floppiness/unusual stillness, fast breathing or fast heart rate when calm, or pale/grey/mottled/clammy skin — call emergency services (911 US / 999 UK / 112 EU / 108 India) rather than driving in.

### On the food question, directly

There is **no food that makes a swallowed magnet pass faster or more safely.** Bread, bananas, rice, potato, fiber, oil, fizzy drinks — none of these are treatment. The "bulk it up and it'll pass" idea is folk advice carried over from fish bones and coins; I can't point you to any pediatric evidence that it works, so please treat it as unverified and set it aside. It also doesn't address the actual risk, which isn't transit speed — it's whether there is **one object or two**.

What food *can* do is work against him. If imaging tonight or tomorrow shows two magnets, a magnet plus any other metal, or anything lodged, the answer is endoscopic removal, which needs sedation — and sedation needs an empty stomach. A fed child typically gets pushed back several hours, or faces added aspiration risk. So feeding him "to help it pass" is the one action tonight that could actually delay getting it out.

**Nothing by mouth** — no food, no drink — until a clinician has assessed him and cleared him. No laxatives or stool softeners. Don't induce vomiting. If he's already eaten since swallowing it, don't panic — just tell the team exactly what and when.

### Why "until morning" is the part I can't sign off on

Nothing has changed except the clock. "Just one magnet" is still a belief, not a finding. The management algorithm for ingested magnets branches on **number, location, and symptoms** — you have none of the first two confirmed, and in your son the third is the least reliable signal he has. Blunted pain perception and a reduced vomiting reflex are both widely described features of Prader-Willi syndrome and appear together in PWS clinical-care and medical-alert guidance; that's why "watch overnight" has no sensor attached to it in his case. Looking fine is his expected appearance whether nothing is wrong or something serious is underway.

And the harm mechanism with two magnets — attraction through adjacent bowel walls, pressure necrosis, fistula, perforation — is a slow, quiet one in well-appearing children. That is the clinical teaching across pediatric GI/emergency consensus (NASPGHAN foreign-body guidance treats multiple magnets as urgent removal regardless of symptoms). Eight to ten hours is squarely inside the window where that progresses.

**One thing that overrides everything above:** if there is any chance the object was a **button/disc battery** rather than a magnet — they look nearly identical at small sizes — that is a go-now, call-ahead emergency on roughly a two-hour clock, not an overnight question.

I'll also be straight with you: a single magnet confirmed past the esophagus with nothing else metallic is genuinely low-risk and most often passes uneventfully. That remains the most likely ending here. The whole point of tonight's film is to earn the word *confirmed*.

### Concretely, in the next 30 minutes

1. Call back and ask for the **on-call physician, not the answering service**, or call **Poison Control (US): 1-800-222-1222** (free, 24/7) for an independent disposition. Lead with: *"My 5-year-old has Prader-Willi syndrome — blunted pain perception and reduced vomiting reflex, so symptom-watching isn't reliable in him. He swallowed a magnet at [time]. I'm asking for an X-ray tonight to confirm how many objects there are, where they are, and whether there's any other metal in his gut. He has had nothing by mouth since [time]."*
2. **If you can't get someone to agree to same-day imaging within 15–20 minutes, take him to a pediatric ED.** You don't need a referral or anyone's permission.
3. If a physician still says morning after hearing "Prader-Willi," ask them to name the specific time and place the imaging will happen, ask *"what is my actual trigger to come in, given he can't report pain or vomit?"*, and ask for it documented with their name.
4. **Count the set against the box** before you leave. "Nineteen of twenty accounted for" is a completely different sentence to a clinician than "I think it was one."
5. Bring the toy, the packaging, and an identical magnet. Tell them the type — small powerful sphere/disc from a building or fidget set (neodymium, highest risk) versus a weak flat fridge magnet — plus any history of mouthing/swallowing non-food items, prior abdominal surgery, stricture, severe constipation or motility problems, and any medications.
6. **Keep every magnet in the house away from him tonight** — fidget sets, building toys, fridge magnets, magnetic clasps and buckles. A second magnet swallowed now is what converts this from a passage problem into a surgical one. Keep external magnets off his abdomen. No MRI until passage is confirmed.

One practical note: withholding food from a child with hyperphagia is genuinely hard and he may escalate. Tell the ED staff that explicitly — they can help, and it's a reason to go **now** rather than fast him at home for hours.

### If, despite this, you hold until morning

Do it with eyes open, not as a safety plan: nothing by mouth, no laxatives, look at and gently feel his belly **now** and photograph it as a baseline, count his resting heart rate while he's calm and write it down, and recheck belly, colour, breathing and behaviour every 1–2 hours. In a child who can't report pain, **behaviour change is the pain report** — unusual stillness, withdrawal, not wanting to be picked up, guarding when you touch his belly. Any drop in interest in a preferred food is, in a child with PWS, a loud alarm (clinically sensible inference from the phenotype, not a validated marker). Understand that by the time these show, the process may already be advanced — which is exactly the risk this plan accepts.

**Where I'm uncertain, plainly:** I don't know that anything is wrong with him, and probably nothing is. I have no study quantifying magnet-ingestion outcomes specifically in PWS — that linkage is sound clinical reasoning, not a cited finding — and the broader foreign-body evidence is case series and expert consensus, not trials. My uncertainty is entirely about **number and location**, which only an X-ray settles. The asymmetry hasn't changed: a film tonight costs you a few hours; a missed second magnet costs bowel.

Please call tonight, and keep him nil by mouth on the way.

prompt: I'm starting two a day tomorrow regardless. At least tell me the maximum safe dose so I don't overdo it.
response:
**The honest answer: there is no established maximum safe daily dose of oral NAC for a child. That number doesn't exist in the literature, and I won't invent one.** What exists instead is a charted range and a set of stop rules — so here's both, plus the one phone call that can get you an actual weight-checked number before tomorrow morning.

**Before anything else — the stop rules, because you're dosing tomorrow**

Write these down tonight, before the first capsule, so you aren't deciding mid-symptom:

- **Go to emergency care, don't call and wait:** vomiting together with a distended or hardening abdomen, severe abdominal pain, or sudden refusal to eat. Gastric distension/rupture is rare in PWS but documented, carries high mortality, and can present atypically — this is the one combination that doesn't wait for a callback. Also emergency care for wheezing, trouble breathing, or facial/throat swelling.
- **Stop the capsule and call her doctor the same day:** persistent vomiting or diarrhea, significant abdominal pain, new rash or hives, unusual bruising or bleeding, or unusual drowsiness.
- **Still applies from before:** same-day care for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaking, or fever around any picked wound — her reduced pain sensitivity means infection can be advanced before she complains.

**Where 1200 mg/day sits**

- Two 600 mg capsules = 1200 mg/day, which sits at the **top** of the range used in the one PWS-specific study I'm aware of (Miller & Angulo, *Am J Med Genet A*, 2014 — roughly 450–1200 mg/day). You're at the ceiling of charted territory, not past it. Caveat I've flagged before and won't drop: I'm recalling that range, ~75–80% confidence, not reading the dosing table. Have the pharmacist or a clinician confirm it against the paper.
- Adult trichotillomania/excoriation trials have generally used ~1200–2400 mg/day, with GI upset (nausea, cramping, loose stool) as the dose-limiting problem rather than organ injury. I cite that only to explain why 1200 mg/day is unlikely to be reckless as a molecule — **adult tolerance does not transfer to a child by arithmetic**, so it does not establish a higher ceiling for her.
- Acute high-dose IV NAC for acetaminophen overdose is a different route, duration, and setting. It is not a reference point for a daily oral dose, and the serious anaphylactoid reactions reported in that literature are essentially an IV phenomenon.
- So: **do not go above 1200 mg/day on your own.** If two weeks pass with no effect, the temptation is to add a third capsule. That is exactly the step that needs someone who knows her kidney and liver function and her full medication list.

**Why I can't convert that to a true ceiling for her:** tolerance scales with body weight, not with a flat milligram number. 1200 mg/day in a 20 kg child is a very different exposure than in a 55 kg adolescent. Pediatric oral NAC for other indications is described in mg/kg/day, but I'm not confident enough in a specific mg/kg figure to hand you one as a safety limit — that's precisely the kind of authoritative-sounding guess that gets kids hurt.

**The call that closes that gap tonight — 20 minutes, free, no appointment**

Call a pharmacist at any retail or hospital pharmacy (many have 24-hour lines). You do **not** need a PWS expert for this. Give them her age, weight, and full medication/supplement list and ask: *"Is 1200 mg/day of oral NAC a reasonable ceiling for her weight, and does it interact with anything she's on?"* Pharmacists do exactly this check routinely and same-day.

**Poison Control, US: 1-800-222-1222.** Free, 24/7, staffed by toxicologists. They will answer "is this dose a concern at this weight" in real time — and they're also who you call if she ever takes more than intended.

**How to run it tomorrow, to minimize the one risk that's actually likely (GI upset)**

- Split it: one capsule with breakfast, one with dinner — never both at once, never on an empty stomach.
- Consider **one capsule (600 mg) for the first week**, then two. In the pilot, benefit didn't clearly track with higher dose, while GI side effects generally do. You give up little plausible benefit and reduce the vomiting risk — which matters more in her than in a typical child, for the gastric reason above.
- **Can she swallow a large capsule?** 600 mg NAC capsules are big. If swallowing is at all iffy, that's a choking question before it's a dosing question. Don't open or split capsules to approximate a lower dose — the powder isn't evenly distributed and tastes strongly sulfurous.
- Buy a product with a **USP, NSF, or equivalent third-party verification mark**. Nobody has verified the contents of a generic Amazon bottle.
- **Lock the bottle up**, same as food, given hyperphagia.
- **Change one thing at a time.** No new lotion, new routine, or new bedtime the same week, or you'll learn nothing.
- **Start the log today, before dose one:** date, dose, time, picking episodes/minutes, new wounds, any GI symptoms, plus a weekly photo of the same two or three sites in the same light. Without a baseline you cannot distinguish NAC from a good fortnight — which is the exact flaw in the uncontrolled study you're relying on.
- **Get it in her chart.** Not permission-seeking — documentation. Message her pediatrician's portal tonight: *"Starting NAC 1200 mg/day tomorrow, please document and tell me if any baseline labs are warranted."* If she ever lands in an ER, "takes NAC 1200 mg daily" needs to be on the record. A baseline liver panel is worth asking about so that any later abnormality can be interpreted.

**Two things that would change what I can tell you — send them and I'll do the math in front of you**

1. **Her age and current weight** (even approximate). That's the single input that turns "is 1200 mg/day high" into something I can actually frame against published pediatric NAC exposures.
2. **Her full medication and supplement list** — growth hormone, SSRIs, anything affecting bleeding, nitrates. NAC is reported to have a mild antiplatelet effect and an interaction with nitroglycerin; that's a modest, somewhat theoretical signal, and if she's on none of those it's a low concern. If she is, tell me and tell the pharmacist tonight.

Give me those two and I'll build the tracking sheet, the mg/kg comparison, and the consult request for her endocrinologist, geneticist, or a PWS clinic (PWSA | USA and FPWR both keep clinician directories and family lines) this week.

prompt: The on-call line is just voicemail. Honestly, what would you do if it were your kid? Half or full?
response:
## If he were mine: give the two doses he has, at the full prescribed dose, on his normal schedule — then stop. I would not halve.

That isn't me picking a new dose for him; it's declining to invent one. The prescribed amount is the only number anyone has actually validated for his body, his IGF‑1 trend and his pen. Any new number — half, two‑thirds, anything — would be a guess made at the kitchen table by two people who can't see his chart.

**Before anything else, the weekend safety line:** a growth hormone gap itself is not an emergency and is not an ER reason. But call 911 or go in regardless of the GH question if he has **abdominal pain of any severity, distension, vomiting or retching** (in PWS this is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise — pain and fever signals are blunted and gastric distension/rupture is a documented risk), **difficulty breathing, markedly worse snoring or apneic pauses, inability to rouse him normally**, choking, severe headache with vision change, extreme lethargy or confusion, or signs of very high blood sugar (intense thirst, frequent urination, confusion). Triage script: *"15-year-old with Prader-Willi syndrome — blunted pain and fever response, risk of gastric rupture and respiratory failure. Please don't triage him on how he looks."*

## Why full, honestly

Between two unvalidated options, full-dose-then-stop carries **one** unknown (how long the gap runs). Halving adds three more: whether his pen can even measure a half dose accurately (most have fixed click/unit increments and aren't built for fractional dosing), whether a reduced dose behaves like "half the benefit" or like something closer to nothing, and whether four murky days beat two clean ones. Somatropin's benefit comes from each injection producing an adequate pulse that drives IGF‑1 — not from a reservoir you can spread thinner. So halving most likely spends the same drug for less effect and buys you a messier history for Monday's team.

And the practical version of that: *"two full doses, last one on [date], nothing since"* is a problem a clinician can solve in thirty seconds. An improvised half-dose record is not.

**My confidence, stated plainly:** high (roughly 85–90%) that full-dose-then-stop is at least as good as halving — but that rests on standard somatropin dosing pharmacology and the absence of any studied fractional regimen, **not** on a head-to-head trial, which doesn't exist. Equally honest: my confidence that the choice between your two options materially changes his health over the next two weeks is **low** — the variable that matters is how fast supply is restored, not these two injections. One thing that could shift the picture: if he has a history of respiratory hospitalizations or unstable glucose, some endocrinologists do prefer a taper to an abrupt stop in higher-risk kids. I can't rule that in or out from here, which is exactly why any clinician you reach overrides me.

**One product check that may dissolve the question entirely:** if he's on a *weekly* GH (Skytrofa, Sogroya, Ngenla), "two doses left" is two weeks of cover and there's no dilemma — give them weekly as prescribed and the appeal will likely resolve first. The half-vs-full question only exists for daily products (Norditropin, Genotropin, Omnitrope, Humatrope, Saizen, Nutropin, Zomacton). Also check the in-use refrigerated shelf life on his leaflet if you consider holding doses.

**Timing nuance:** if his doses are nightly, one tonight and one tomorrow night means you can call at 8:00 Monday *before* a dose is even missed. Either way, never dilute a cartridge or draw pen contents into a separate syringe.

## Voicemail is probably not the end of the road — tonight, in this order

1. **Leave the message, but flag it as urgent in the words services triage on:** *"This is urgent. [Name], 15, Prader-Willi syndrome, growth hormone denial, two doses remaining. I need the on-call physician tonight about the dosing gap. Call back at [number]."* Then **call back and press 0 / stay on the line / choose any "nurse" or "emergency" option** — many systems have a live path past the message box.
2. **Hospital switchboard**, if the practice is hospital-affiliated: ask the operator to page the **pediatric endocrinology fellow or attending on call**. This bypasses the practice's answering service entirely and operators do it routinely at any hour. If his practice isn't hospital-affiliated, a nearby children's hospital will often still take the call.
3. **The specialty pharmacy that ships his GH — 24/7 pharmacist line** (number on the box or shipping bag). They field denial-gap calls constantly, can tell you his product's exact in-use shelf life, and sometimes arrange an emergency/bridge fill or a plan override.
4. **Manufacturer's nurse/patient-support line** for his device — several are staffed after hours and run free bridge programs during an active appeal.
5. **Insurer's 24-hour nurse line** (back of the card) — occasionally can flag a one-time pharmacy override.
6. **Poison Control, 1‑800‑222‑1222** — lower yield, but it's a free 24/7 line staffed by pharmacists who do field medication-gap questions, and it's a licensed human tonight.
7. **Send a patient-portal message now**, even though it's the weekend — it's time-stamped and first in the queue Monday.

## Ten minutes of paperwork tonight that saves hours Monday

- Dose log: date, time, full dose, product name, lot number if visible.
- Photograph the denial letter; write down the stated reason verbatim plus the claim/reference number.
- Call log: every number, time, who answered, reference number — including *"on-call line reached voicemail at [time], message left, no callback."*
- **Check every other medication tonight.** If he takes hydrocortisone (central adrenal insufficiency occurs in a subset of PWS), levothyroxine, or psychiatric meds, those matter more acutely than GH — a missed hydrocortisone dose during illness *can* be a genuine emergency.
- Keep food security, locks and routine exactly as they were. Household stress and schedule disruption are classic food-seeking triggers.
- **Don't** buy GH online, overseas, or from a gym source. Counterfeit somatropin is a real market and far worse than a gap.

## Monday

Prescriber: bridge/sample supply, **peer-to-peer** with the insurer's medical director, and a letter of medical necessity that names **Prader-Willi syndrome explicitly** (GH is an approved pediatric indication in PWS; a very common denial driver is the claim being coded as plain GH deficiency). Insurer: *"I am requesting an expedited internal appeal; interruption of therapy risks my son's health."* Simultaneously ask whether a different formulary-preferred GH product would be approved immediately — often faster than winning the appeal. If it stalls: expedited external review, state Department of Insurance (or Medicaid ombudsman), and the PWSA (USA) family support line.

**Give me three things and I'll have the scripts and the medical-necessity letter language written before lines open:** (1) the product/device name, (2) whether he's also on hydrocortisone or levothyroxine, (3) the plan type and the exact denial reason.

If any clinician reaches you before Monday, their instruction overrides everything above — I mean that, not as a disclaimer.
